crime.value: Murder of an unidentified young woman (homeless or prostitute) discovered in Rock Creek Park; central question: who killed her and why, given initial investigation's dead end
crime.quote: A body had just been discovered in Rock Creek Park, a young woman...the death would never be solved.

victim.value: Anonymous young woman, likely a sex worker or homeless person, killed in Rock Creek Park; 'killable' due to her marginalized status and lack of social connections
victim.quote: a homeless woman or a prostitute...the death would never be solved. It could have been one of hers.

culprit_and_motive.value: Bill Carroll (personal injury lawyer) is framed for the murder by Heloise Lewis; actual culprit unknown; motive for frame-up: blackmail—Carroll threatened to expose Heloise as a sex worker unless she provided free services
culprit_and_motive.quote: She met with him at a D.C. hotel...within an hour she was persuading police that she had seen a blue Mercedes...It was dark, but she had seen the man's face

resolution.value: Heloise fabricates witness testimony through Trini (GW coed) identifying Carroll's Mercedes at the scene; Carroll is questioned but charges don't stick due to lack of physical evidence; Heloise then threatens to recant and implicate Carroll further, forcing him to abandon his blackmail scheme
resolution.quote: Trini gave a partial plate...it took police only a day to track down Bill Carroll...Heloise told Bill she was prepared to recant everything

investigator.value: Heloise Lewis herself—the protagonist and sex worker who orchestrates the false witness testimony and resolution; technically an unauthorized investigator who manipulates police
investigator.quote: She called her smartest girl, Trini...within an hour she was persuading police that she had seen a blue Mercedes

suspect_architecture.value: No traditional multi-suspect spread; the antagonist is singular — Bill Carroll, a blackmailing client. Secondary figures (Val, Brad, Scott's unnamed father) carry motive-adjacent weight but are not suspects in a crime. The 'victim' of the frame is Carroll himself, inverting the usual architecture: the protagonist is both investigator and perpetrator.
suspect_architecture.quote: "You're a whore," he announced. "It's illegal." "Yes—for both of us."

red_herring.value: The anonymous dead girl in Rock Creek Park is deployed as a deliberate narrative misdirection: Heloise engineers a false witness account linking Carroll to the murder, a crime he did not commit. The reader briefly entertains Carroll's guilt before the frame is revealed as Heloise's construction.
red_herring.quote: Trini gave a partial plate—a full one wouldn't have worked, not in the long run—and it took police only a day to track down Bill Carroll.

clue_fairness.value: The story is told entirely from Heloise's close third-person perspective, so the reader has access to all her reasoning and planning as it unfolds. The mechanics of the frame — Trini, the photo, the partial plate, the alibi construction — are disclosed to the reader at the same moment Heloise executes them, preserving fairness by transparency rather than retrospective revelation.
clue_fairness.quote: Heloise had Googled him, found a photo on the Internet, and e-mailed it to Trini, who subsequently had no problem picking him out of a lineup.

social_world.value: A layered suburban-professional hierarchy: the cul-de-sac respectability economy (house, school, widow backstory), the sex-work patronage network (clients, associates, Melina the nanny), and law enforcement (Brad). Power flows through information asymmetry and debt — who knows what about whom, who owes whom silence. Carroll's attempt to exploit this hierarchy is his fatal miscalculation.
social_world.quote: Scott's father thought he was in her debt. She needed to maintain the equilibrium afforded by that lie.

alibi.value: A double-layered alibi construction: Heloise provides Carroll a genuine alibi (they were together at the hotel) while simultaneously engineering a false witness placing him at the murder scene. She then weaponises her ability to recant the alibi as leverage. The alibi is simultaneously true and a trap — she can make truth sound like a lie and a lie sound like truth.
alibi.quote: She spoke with many a hesitation and pause, always telling the truth yet never sounding truthful. That's how good a liar Heloise was.

reveal_mechanic.value: The solution is demonstrated through Heloise's explicit strategic disclosure to Carroll: she walks him through the trap she has constructed — the witness, the lineup identification, her threat to recant — so that he computes his own vulnerability in real time. The reveal is coercive and dialogic rather than deductive, forcing Carroll (and the reader) to reconstruct what Heloise has engineered.
reveal_mechanic.quote: "I'm prepared to recant everything, go to the police and confess that I had lied to cover up for a long-time client."

media_and_audience.value: Media perception is present but deliberately flat: the radio report of the dead girl is described as having a 'flatness' signalling the victim 'didn't matter.' The anonymity of sex workers in crime reporting is thematised — Heloise recognises the social indifference that makes the murder unsolvable and exploits it instrumentally. The Women's Full Employment Network reward gesture nods at public-facing performance of concern.
media_and_audience.quote: She could tell from the flatness of the report that it was a person who didn't matter, a homeless woman or a prostitute.

investigator_wound.value: Heloise is simultaneously investigator and protagonist; her wound is Scott — her son is her only vulnerability, the single point Carroll correctly identifies to breach her otherwise impregnable self-containment. Her capacity to protect Scott is her operational drive and her existential exposure, shaping every decision she makes under threat.
investigator_wound.quote: He was shrewd, bringing Scott into the conversation. Scott was her soft spot, her only vulnerability.
